factors.name: Delivered output versus artifacts about output
factors.question: How much definition mass exists per unit of thing the definitions exist to produce, is the ratio moving toward delivery, and is there a declared appetite that could ever trip a circuit breaker?
factors.measurement: Partition every word, commit and hour into (A) product-facing output consumed outside the system that produced it, (B) definitions/process/tooling about how work is done, (C) records about work done. Report (B+C)/total weekly so the derivative is visible, plus elapsed days ÷ declared appetite. Re-run baselines (verified 2026-09-17): `find basis -name '*.md' | wc -l` → 115 files; `cat $(find basis -name '*.md') | wc -w` → 159,891 words; plus ~130k more words in requests/, briefs/, decisions/, features/, initiatives/, sessions/; `find . -name '*.py' | xargs wc -l` → 4,461 lines, all of it corpus compilers, linters and cost rollups (basis/tools/); 280 commits since 2026-08-22; product-facing software: zero. A = 0, so the ratio is 1.0. Then: count efforts with a written appetite, efforts past appetite, and of those how many were cancelled rather than extended — Shape Up's circuit breaker leaves a record of things killed; no such record in 26 days means the model is cited, not in force.
factors.sources: Agile Manifesto, Principles 1/3/7 — "Working software is the primary measure of progress" (https://agilemanifesto.org/principles.html); Ryan Singer, Shape Up ch. 6 (appetite) and ch. 8 ("If they don't finish, by default the project doesn't get an extension") — https://basecamp.com/shapeup/2.2-chapter-08; Hamel & Zanini, "What We Learned About Bureaucracy from 7,000 HBR Readers", HBR Aug 2017 (insularity = effort on internal rather than external issues) — https://hbr.org/2017/08/what-we-learned-about-bureaucracy-from-7000-hbr-readers; Dan Ward, The Simplicity Cycle (2015) — complexity raises goodness to an inflection point and lowers it after.

factors.name: Coverage of the built artifact versus coverage of the procedure
factors.question: Does the corpus say anywhere what a good built thing looks like, or only who does what, in what order, checked by whom?
factors.measurement: Classify every directive as artifact-quality (a property of the thing produced: decomposition, interfaces, failure behaviour, performance, security, readability) or process-quality (sequence, record, role, check). Report the ratio per principle set and corpus-wide. Then map the corpus onto ISO/IEC 25010:2023's nine characteristics and count how many are addressed with stated criteria. Coverage test: take five questions a maker actually asks — how do I decompose this, what belongs behind an interface, how should errors surface, when is duplication acceptable, what does done mean for this scenario — and count how many the corpus answers. Verified baseline: `grep -ril <term> basis --include='*.md'` gives maintainability 0, modular 0, cohesion 0, reliability 0, security 0, coupling 1, performance 3, testab* 5, observab* 5 files. All six implementation principles (built-to-the-scenario, effect-shown, effect-not-mechanism, nothing-lost, knowable-from-the-record, cost-on-the-initiative) govern scope, evidence and accounting; none states a property of well-built software.
factors.sources: ISO/IEC 25010:2023, Systems and software engineering — SQuaRE — Product quality model, nine characteristics (https://www.iso.org/standard/78176.html; 2023 change summary https://quality.arc42.org/articles/iso-25010-update-2023); TOGAF Architecture Principles, "Complete" and "Robust" criteria (https://pubs.opengroup.org/architecture/togaf92-doc/arch/chap20.html); Jeff Bezos, 2017 Letter to Shareholders — "high standards are teachable" only if people can "recognize what excellence looks like in a domain" (https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/2017-letter-to-shareholders).

factors.name: Enforcement locus: tooled gate versus prose rule
factors.question: For each obligation, what actually stops a violation — a schema, a tool, a failing test — or only a sentence the agent is asked to remember?
factors.measurement: Tabulate every normative statement against its enforcement level: (1) structurally impossible to violate, (2) blocked by tool/schema/lint at write time, (3) detected automatically after the fact, (4) checked by a fresh-context agent against stated criteria, (5) prose only, self-attested. Report the distribution, and for every level 4–5 rule ask whether a violation produces any signal at all. Verified baseline: 127 MUST/MUST NOT statements in basis/ (`grep -rho '\bMUST\b' basis --include='*.md' | wc -l` → 106; MUST NOT → 21) against basis/tools/lint_basis.py, whose entire rule surface is ~53 definitions/error sites — i.e. most obligations sit at level 4–5. Second count: obligations that are about form, presence, naming, sequence or completeness (a linter's natural class) but are enforced by prose — each one is context spent on something a program could enforce at zero context cost.
factors.sources: Anthropic, "Building effective agents" (Dec 2024) — "Poka-yoke your tools. Change the arguments so that it is harder to make mistakes" (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents); Anthropic, "Effective harnesses for long-running agents" — structure the environment rather than the prompt; forbid status changes until an external test runs; OpenAI, "A practical guide to building agents" (Apr 2025), layered guardrails mixing deterministic and model-based checks (https://cdn.openai.com/business-guides-and-resources/a-practical-guide-to-building-agents.pdf); Zhou et al., IFEval, arXiv:2311.07911 — the tractable instruction class is the programmatically verifiable one.

factors.name: Constraint integrity: who can waive, who can stamp
factors.question: Can the party a constraint binds relieve itself of that constraint, or declare its own work compliant, without any other party acting?
factors.measurement: Build the unrule register. Table: constraint | binds whom | who may waive | waivers in the last 30 days | where the waiver is recorded | expiry | ever revisited. Grep the corpus and working artifacts for `accepted gap`, `accepted tradeoff`, `exception`, `waiver`, `deferred`, `out of scope for now`, `not repaired`, and for self-asserted fitness-pass tables. Report (a) unrules per obligation, (b) share invoked by the same role the obligation constrains, (c) share with no expiry and no owner, (d) age of each. Separately classify every check's checker as: same agent, different role but same generating context and same interest in passing, fresh context with different accountability, or external. Then the asymmetry test: process weight to impose an obligation (draft, guideline, fitness set, independent judge, owner approval) versus process weight to lift one. Verified baseline: `grep -ro 'self-check' --include='*.md' . | wc -l` → 196 occurrences; `accepted gap` appears across 8 files including basis/artifacts/feature.md and six feature records; basis/principles.md follows its self-asserted fitness screen with an "Accepted tradeoffs" section recording known violations of the set's own rules and declining repair; features are set `checked` by the PO that authored them; the artifact tooling exists but nothing prevents a raw sed/grep edit around it (greppable in session transcripts).
factors.sources: Coglianese, Scheffler & Walters, "Unrules", 73 Stan. L. Rev. 885 (2021) — "A regulatory system can be understood only as the net effects of both its rules and its unrules"; constraints on imposing obligations exceed constraints on lifting them (https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2021/04/Coglianese-et-al.-73-Stan.-L.-Rev.-885.pdf); IIA, The Three Lines Model (July 2020) — assurance requires independence from the activity assessed (https://www.theiia.org/globalassets/documents/resources/the-iias-three-lines-model-an-update-of-the-three-lines-of-defense-july-2020/three-lines-model-updated-english.pdf); ISO 9001 cl. 9.2 / ISO 19011 impartiality; Cai et al., "Rule Taxonomy and Evolution in AI IDEs", arXiv:2606.12231 — baseline artifact compliance with stated rules 49.14% across 83 projects and 7,310 rules.

factors.name: Feedback from outcome back to specification
factors.question: For any definition in this corpus, is there a recorded before/after outcome showing it changed behaviour for the better — and does any error signal reach the corpus from outside the corpus?
factors.measurement: Count definitions with any outcome measure attached (an A/B, a before/after defect or compliance count, a rework count), as a percentage of all definitions. Record time since each definition's last outcome measurement and the number of revisions made with no outcome evidence. Count the eval fixtures that exist at all — representative tasks the corpus can be run against. Then classify every indicator the system uses (approvals granted, checks passed, fitness screens cleared, self-checks recorded) as self-reported by the measured party or independently observed, and plot each against any externally observable outcome. Verified baseline: 18 features, 16 initiatives, 10 ADRs, 8 PDRs, 41 requests, 29 session records — every recorded indicator is internal and self-reported; the only external observable (shipped software) is flat at zero, so no indicator can be correlated with anything outside the loop.
factors.sources: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov & Suhr, "Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design", ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.11324 — semantically equivalent formatting variants swing accuracy up to 76 points, so untested wording is an untested intervention; Gloaguen et al., "Evaluating AGENTS.md", arXiv:2602.11988 — context files gave no general success gain at >20% inference cost; "any attempts to improve performance should be rigorously evaluated before deployment"; Agrawal et al., GEPA, arXiv:2507.19457 and Zhou et al., APE, arXiv:2211.01910 — author intuition about instruction wording is a poor predictor; V. F. Ridgway, "Dysfunctional Consequences of Performance Measurements", ASQ 1(2) 1956; Meyer & Rowan, AJS 83(2) 1977 — decoupling sustained by a "logic of confidence".

factors.name: Form fit: rule, standard or principle — and does the form match the traffic?
factors.question: For each normative statement, was its content fixed in advance (a rule) or left to be given content at the point of application (a standard/principle) — does that choice match how often and how uniformly the situation arises, and can the corpus express any form but the rule?
factors.measurement: Tabulate every normative statement. (a) Classify rule vs standard: can a reader decide compliance from the text alone, or must someone judge at the moment of use? (b) Count actual applications in the last 30 days from the working artifacts — how many times did this statement bind real work? Score two mismatch buckets: rules applied 0–2 times (content fixed in advance for traffic that never came; report their total word cost) and standards applied 20+ times (the same judgment re-litigated every session). (c) Classify every directive into Sunstein's forms — untrammeled discretion, rules, rules with excuses, presumptions, factors, standards, guidelines, principles — and report the histogram; count how many forms the corpus can express at all. A corpus with no presumption, no factor list, and no documented-departure guideline has a one-form grammar. (d) Report the share of directives labelled "principle" that are in fact rules by Sunstein's test; in this corpus the principle-set typedef's own construction (a principle as a standing rule, statements binary-testable on one artifact) makes that share close to 100% by design. (e) Search Document History and briefs for guidance-style content dropped because it would not fit the rule form.
factors.sources: Louis Kaplow, "Rules versus Standards: An Economic Analysis", 42 Duke L.J. 557 (1992), pp. 560, 577, 599–600 — "the only distinction between rules and standards is the extent to which efforts to give content to the law are undertaken before or after individuals act"; "the greater the frequency with which a legal command will apply, the more desirable rules tend to be relative to standards" (https://scholarship.law.duke.edu/dlj/vol42/iss3/2/); Cass R. Sunstein, "Problems with Rules", 83 Calif. L. Rev. 953 (1995), pp. 959–68 — "a principle is a background notion that does not by itself cover an individual case... principles tend to bear on cases without disposing of them" (p. 966); "If a standard is transparent... it is a rule" (p. 965) (https://scholarship.law.berkeley.edu/californialawreview/vol83/iss4/1/); TOGAF Architecture Principles, "Consistent" — the set "must be expressed in a way that allows a balance of interpretations".

factors.name: Obligation load per activity, for the human and the model reader
factors.question: How many independently checkable obligations bind one step at once, how much text must be traversed to find them, and does adherence hold at that count?
factors.measurement: Count obligations, not sentences: every clause a checker could independently mark pass/fail that binds this step — compiled principle bullets, guideline writing rules, typedef fields, fitness criteria, step prompt directives. Sum per step and record which are always-on (inherited) versus local; flag any step whose always-on share exceeds ~30% of its load. Report words per obligation, mean sentence length and sentences over 30 words, and the structural-overhead ratio: words about the corpus's own mechanics (types, chains, renderings, compilations, load points) over words about the product or the work. Then run the empirical half: take 10 recent outputs produced under that context, score each against every obligation, and compare against the same agent given only the 5 most load-bearing obligations — if the extra rules buy no measurable quality, they are cost with no yield. Verified baselines: 25 process definitions totalling 63,009 words; normative keywords in basis/ 106 MUST, 21 MUST NOT, 5 SHOULD, 0 SHOULD NOT, 13 MAY (absolute share 88%, MUST:SHOULD ≈ 21:1); repo-wide 157/28/5/13 (absolute share 91%). Note the researchers' counts differ from mine (129/28 vs 106/21) depending on scope — re-run the grep and state the scope rather than inheriting a number. Apply RFC 2119 §6 to a sample of MUSTs: does this exist for interoperation between roles or to prevent harm, or is it method imposition?
factors.sources: UK Office of the Parliamentary Counsel, Drafting Guidance (March 2024) 1.1.11 ("one idea per sentence"), 1.1.13–14 ("The medium is not the message"), 1.3.2 (Gowers) — https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/660407d091a320001a82b06b/2024.03.19.Drafting-guidance.pdf; Jaroslawicz et al., IFScale, arXiv:2507.11538 — adherence degrades steadily with instruction count, omission errors dominating, with primacy bias toward earlier instructions; Kimura et al., ManyIFEval, EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv:2509.21051 — all-instructions-satisfied accuracy predictable from count alone; Anthropic, "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (Sept 2025) — "the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens" (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents); RFC 2119 §6 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.txt); Al-Ubaydli & McLaughlin, RegData, Regulation & Governance 11(1) 2017 — restriction counts track burden better than page counts.

factors.name: Rejection power and contestability
factors.question: Shown the last 20–30 pieces of real work, how much would each principle have turned away — how much did it actually turn away on the record — and could a competent peer shop defend its opposite?
factors.measurement: Two numbers per principle: hypothetical rejection rate (of the last 20–30 delivered artifacts, how many would it have rejected) and observed rejection rate (a check that failed and cited this principle, a review finding, a rewrite). Spool's benchmark is roughly two-thirds hypothetical; an observed rate of zero over the whole corpus history means the principle has never changed an output. Then contestability: write each principle's negation as a one-line position and score contested (a named real practice holds it and survives) / permission-to-play (no competent shop would hold the negation) / vacuous (the negation is unintelligible). Cheap proxies: count principles whose statement contains no trade-off ("rather than", "over", "instead of", a named cost accepted); count obligations per principle statement (five MUST bullets is five stands, not one); count principles whose rationale contains no concrete failure example. Structural hazard to flag here: basis/guidelines/principle-set.md forbids grounding a rationale in the product's own operational history — which is precisely the evidence Spool's Test #1 demands, so no principle in this corpus can prove it came from research.
factors.sources: Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design Principles: 6 Counter-Intuitive Tests" — Test #1 comes from research, Test #2 "Does it Help You Say 'No' Most of the Time?", Test #4 reversibility (https://articles.centercentre.com/creating-design-principles/); Patrick Lencioni, "Make Your Values Mean Something", HBR July 2002 — permission-to-play values "never really help distinguish a company" and bland sets are "highly destructive" (https://hbr.org/2002/07/make-your-values-mean-something); Charlie Kindel, "Tenets" (2020) — a tenet "takes a stand by declaring that a team cares more about one thing than another" (https://blog.kindel.com/2020/02/10/tenets/); Richard Rumelt, Good Strategy / Bad Strategy (2011) — fluff, "Sunday words", the guiding policy that "directs and constrains action without fully defining it".

factors.name: Check economics: does each check pay, and is its verdict reproducible?
factors.question: What fraction of effort goes into checking rather than making, how often does each check actually fail anything, and would a fresh context re-checking the same artifact reach the same verdict?
factors.measurement: Per standing check: items checked in the last 30 days, items failed, hours spent, estimated cost of an escape. Defect fraction p = failed ÷ checked; compare against Deming's kp break-even (inspect none if p < k1/k2). A check with a 100% historical pass rate is either redundant with the making step or performed pro forma. Count check steps per process definition and the number of distinct checks one artifact passes end to end; count checks that cannot cite the clause they enforce. Then reproducibility: take 5 artifacts recorded as passing, re-run the stated check in a fresh context with no access to the original verdict, and report the agreement rate (healthy ≥80%, red <60%) and whether the check can be re-run at all or exists only as a prose assertion. Same test as an inter-reader agreement measure: 10 rules × 10 artifacts, two fresh contexts, yes/no verdict plus the clause relied on — rules under ~80% agreement are standards wearing a rule's clothes, paying a rule's promulgation cost and a standard's interpretation cost. Verified baseline: every process definition in basis/processes/ ends in or contains check steps (`grep -c check` ranges 2–63 per file across 25 files); basis/architecture-principles.md and basis/implementation-principles.md each end in an in-document fitness screen whose rows read "pass", asserted by the author — an unreproducible pass by construction.
factors.sources: W. Edwards Deming, Out of the Crisis (1986), Point 3 — "Cease dependence on inspection... build quality into the product in the first place" (https://deming.org/explore/fourteen-points/) and the kp all-or-none inspection criterion, J. Quality Technology 17(3) 1985; Michael Power, The Audit Society: Rituals of Verification (OUP 1997) — audit produces comfort rather than knowledge and "self-referentially creat[es] auditable images of performance"; Cemri, Pan, Yang et al., MAST, arXiv:2503.13657 — task-verification failure (premature termination, inadequate verification) is one of three top failure categories over 1,600+ annotated traces; Julia Black, "Forms and Paradoxes of Principles Based Regulation", LSE WP 13/2008, pp. 22–24, 29–31 — the interpretive and enforcement paradoxes; Colin S. Diver, "The Optimal Precision of Administrative Rules", 93 Yale L.J. 65 (1983).

factors.name: Flow efficiency, the single-human constraint, and batch size
factors.question: Of the elapsed time from a request entering to something leaving, what fraction added value — how much of that elapsed time was queued in front of the one human, and how big is the unit of work between contacts with reality?
factors.measurement: Take 5 completed items end to end from commit and session timestamps; mark each interval touch or wait (waiting on approval, clarification, a check, a rendering). Flow efficiency = touch ÷ elapsed (practitioner reference band: 5–15% typical, 15–25% good; treat as a within-system trend, not a gate). Governance variant: fraction of touch time spent on the item versus on satisfying the process about the item — red if the second exceeds the first. Constraint: count process steps requiring the authority's decision as a share of all steps; items waiting on that person; mean wait per approval; and the split of the authority's attention between irreducible decisions (bets, direction, priority) and reducible clarifications (what does this rule mean, does this satisfy that). The discriminator is the trend in clarification share across successive artifacts — falling means the corpus is maturing, flat or rising means each new definition buys ambiguity at least as fast as it resolves it. Batch size: how many artifacts are approved in one decision (this corpus approved the product flow end to end "by batch under brief-032"), and the interval between a corpus change and any external validation — currently unbounded, since nothing has executed. Alongside these, record the authority's own standing self-report (is this getting easier or harder; what fraction of last cycle moved the product): in a one-human system that perception is the outcome variable, not anecdote.
factors.sources: Eliyahu Goldratt, The Goal (1984) and the Five Focusing Steps, esp. "subordinate" — non-constraints must not run faster than the constraint (https://www.tocinstitute.org/five-focusing-steps.html); Kanban University, "Flow Efficiency" (https://resources.kanban.university/flow-efficiency-a-great-metric-you-probably-arent-using/); Donald Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) — batch size economics and invisible queues; Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Houck & Butler, "The SPACE of Developer Productivity", ACM Queue 19(1) 2021 — use at least three dimensions, never one metric, include perceptual data (https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3454124).

factors.name: Ceremonial mass: definitions never executed, rules never retired
factors.question: How many defined processes have actually run end to end, how long after approval did the first run happen, and how many obligations have ever been removed?
factors.measurement: Per definition: date approved → date first executed end to end; number of complete executions; date of last execution; steps skipped in the most recent execution; and whether any record asserts a step ran that left no artifact. Compute never-run share (red flag >40%) and median definition-to-execution lag. From version control, count obligations added, amended and removed per week and compute the retirement ratio = removals ÷ additions; also rule half-life (median age at first revisit). A monotonic rule count is the expected null trajectory for any rule-making system, so the retirement ratio is the only observable separating learning from silting. Verified baseline: 25 process definitions, 63,009 words; several (implementation, scenario-assignment, reconcile-and-close, the bc-emit and mailbox paths) are unexecutable by construction while the shop is frozen, yet stand fully specified and approved; git history over 280 commits shows additive approval batches and no recorded retirement event in the corpus's own terms — retirement exists only as a planned migration action. Also apply Bozeman's test to 10 randomly sampled obligations: name one concrete failure this rule prevented in the last 30 days, with the record that shows it; red-tape share = (unserved + unknown) ÷ 10.
factors.sources: James G. March, Martin Schulz & Xueguang Zhou, The Dynamics of Rules: Change in Written Organizational Codes (Stanford UP, 2000) — rule birth is easy, rule suspension rare (https://www.sup.org/books/title/?id=388); Barry Bozeman, Bureaucracy and Red Tape (2000) — red tape as rules that "remain in force and entail a compliance burden but [do] not advance the legitimate purposes the rules were intended to serve"; rule-inception versus rule-evolved red tape (overview: https://regulatorystudies.columbian.gwu.edu/red-tape-literature-public-administration); John W. Meyer & Brian Rowan, "Institutionalized Organizations: Formal Structure as Myth and Ceremony", AJS 83(2) 1977 — ceremonial adoption and decoupling of formal structure from activity.

factors.name: Fidelity of adopted external forms
factors.question: Where the corpus cites an external standard, does it adopt that standard as the source defines it, and is every narrowing, inversion or home-grown addition recorded as a reasoned departure?
factors.measurement: For each external source the corpus names, put the source's own criteria in one column and the corpus's rendering in the next; mark each adopted / narrowed / inverted / dropped, and require a recorded justification for each narrowing. Score fidelity as the share adopted intact. Flag hardest any criterion in a fitness screen that traces to no named source — under the corpus's own external-standards-first principle, a bespoke criterion must be justified by a recorded gap in the form it rejects. Verified starting points in this corpus: basis/fitness/principle-set.fitness.md states its tests "compose TOGAF (statement quality), Spool (helps you say no), Lencioni (not permission-to-play)", and basis/guidelines/principle-set.md cites TOGAF and operational definitions — so check whether TOGAF's Consistent ("allows a balance of interpretations"), Robust and Stable survived; whether Spool's Test #1 (comes from research) survived a guideline that bans product operational history from rationales, and whether Test #4 (reversibility) appears at all; whether BCP 14 was adopted with its §6 necessity limit; and whether any criterion of the form "implies at least one practice and at least one check" has an external parent — that clause is the one that converts a principle set into a generator of process mass.
factors.sources: TOGAF Architecture Principles — the five set-level criteria and the 10–20 heuristic (https://pubs.opengroup.org/architecture/togaf92-doc/arch/chap20.html); Spool's six tests in full (https://articles.centercentre.com/creating-design-principles/); Lencioni's four value types (https://hbr.org/2002/07/make-your-values-mean-something); RFC 2119 §6 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.txt) and RFC 8174 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174.txt); W3C RfcKeywords — keywords attach to a conformance object performing a specified operation (https://www.w3.org/wiki/RfcKeywords); Rumelt's kernel requiring a diagnosis before any guiding policy.

factors.name: Decode cost and findability
factors.question: Can the agent or human who needs a definition find it, parse it, and trust it to be current — or must they reconcile four documents at three levels of a chain to assemble one obligation?
factors.measurement: Task test, not opinion: give a fresh agent 5 real tasks; record time-to-locate the governing definition, number of documents opened, and whether the answer found was current. Multiple documents needing reconciliation to answer one question is a findability failure even when every document is individually correct. Decode cost: take five representative sentences from process definitions and count how many defined terms a reader must already know to parse each — four or more lookups marks the sentence for plain-word rewriting. Per glossary term and schema element: uses outside its own definition (fewer than three marks it for deletion), uses where an ordinary word would carry the same meaning, and any definition that smuggles an obligation into itself rather than stating it as an operative provision. Staleness: share of documents whose stated source-digest or referenced definition no longer matches (this corpus stamps digests, so the check is mechanical). Also classify each paragraph as (a) non-obvious local constraint, (b) restatement of something defined elsewhere in the corpus, (c) restatement of general good practice the model already knows, (d) rationale addressed to humans, and report the (a)-share — the field evidence says (a) is the part that pays and (b)/(c) is the part that costs without paying.
factors.sources: DORA, Capabilities: Documentation quality — clarity, findability, reliability; quality documentation amplifies the organisational-performance effect of every technical capability studied (https://dora.dev/capabilities/documentation-quality/); UK OPC, Drafting Guidance (March 2024) Part 4.1 — avoid misleading labels (4.1.4), avoid bland labels (4.1.5), "Don't make a definition do too much" (4.1.8–9) (https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/660407d091a320001a82b06b/2024.03.19.Drafting-guidance.pdf); Gloaguen et al., "Evaluating AGENTS.md", arXiv:2602.11988 — instructions are followed but repository overviews are not helpful; removing duplicated docs turned a negative into +2.7%; Bryan A. Garner, Legal Writing in Plain English (3rd ed., 2023).

input.rationale:
## Shape of the set

Thirteen factors, ordered so the five foundational ones answer the restart question on their own and the rest explain why. The organising claim is that this corpus has three independent failure surfaces — **what it says** (form and coverage), **what makes it stick** (enforcement and waiver), and **what tells it it is wrong** (outcome feedback and delivery) — and that the third is the one that makes the other two unrecoverable. So `delivery-vs-definition-mass`, `artifact-quality-coverage`, `enforcement-locus`, `constraint-integrity` and `outcome-feedback-loop` are foundational: if all five fail, no per-rule improvement can help, because nothing outside the corpus can tell the corpus it is wrong, nothing in it constrains the product, and nothing but prose holds any rule in place.

Every factor is countable against this repository, and I re-ran the baselines rather than inheriting them. Confirmed on `rebaseline` at 2026-09-17: 115 markdown files / 159,891 words in `basis/`; 25 process definitions totalling 63,009 words; 4,461 lines of Python, all of it corpus compilers, linters and cost rollups; 280 commits since 2026-08-22; zero product-facing software. Normative keywords in `basis/`: **106 MUST, 21 MUST NOT, 5 SHOULD, 0 SHOULD NOT, 13 MAY** (repo-wide 157/28/5/13). The researchers quoted 129/28 — the gap is scope, and I left the exact grep in the measurement so the number is re-derived, not quoted. Quality-attribute vocabulary in `basis/`: maintainability 0 files, modular 0, cohesion 0, reliability 0, security 0, coupling 1, performance 3. `self-check` appears 196 times; `accepted gap` across 8 files. `lint_basis.py` carries roughly 53 rule sites against 127 MUST/MUST NOT statements.

## What I merged

- **Four separate ratio factors** (time to first output, promulgation-to-delivery, meta-work, corpus-to-output) collapse into one, with Shape Up's circuit breaker folded in as a measurement: an appetite nobody can trip is the same finding as a ratio nobody watches.
- **Independence of the check** merged into `constraint-integrity` rather than standing with check economics. Self-approval and self-waiver are one phenomenon: the maker relieving itself. Splitting them lets a system pass one and fail the other while the defect is identical.
- **Reproducibility of a verdict** and **independent-application agreement** are the same experiment (fresh context, same artifact, compare) applied to checks and to rules; they sit together in `check-economics` as its empirical half. That experiment is the single highest-yield thing a reviewer can run here — five re-runs settle an argument that would otherwise run for weeks.
- **Rule-form fit (Kaplow)** and **position on the discretion continuum (Sunstein)** merged into `form-fit`. Kaplow prices the form against traffic; Sunstein names the forms. Separately they invite the trap the cautions warn about — Kaplow alone can be read as "write more rules".
- **Obligation count for models** and **idea density for humans** merged into one factor. They are the same count with two bodies of evidence behind them, and keeping them apart would have implied the corpus could be tuned for one reader at the other's expense.
- **Rule retirement**, **definition-to-execution lag**, **never-run processes** and **red tape** merged into `ceremonial-mass`: all four measure definition written for activity that has not happened and is not disciplined by contact with execution. In a frozen shop with fully specified dispatch, assignment and reconcile processes, this is one finding, not four.

## What I dropped, and why

- **Conflict surface / stated precedence.** Genuine design smell, but the only field study (McMillan, 1,650 sessions) returned an affirmative null for adjacent-file contradiction (BF10 0.05–0.10). A factor whose effect size is contested does not belong in a set that has to carry a restart decision.
- **Prohibition framing.** Self-nominated by its own author as the weakest-sourced factor, resting on practitioner analysis rather than a study. The MUST:SHOULD:MAY count in `obligation-load` already catches the register problem.
- **Within-session compliance decay** as a standalone factor. It is the best-supported field finding in the whole brief (OR 0.944 per generated function) but it rates *how work is scheduled*, not the corpus. It survives as the reason `check-economics` insists on fresh contexts.
- **Instruction altitude** and **output-contract concreteness.** Both are prompt-engineering quality, and both are largely downstream of `form-fit` and `artifact-quality-coverage`: a corpus with no exemplars of a good built thing has no output contract to give.
- **Governance debt ratio (SQALE).** Attractive for the restart arithmetic, but remediation effort is an estimate, and the brief's own rule is that factors deciding a restart must carry hard counts. `delivery-vs-definition-mass` plus `ceremonial-mass` give the same answer from observables.
- **Handoff payload completeness** and **loaded-context budget** as standalone factors, folded into `obligation-load` (always-on share) and `check-economics` (fresh-context carrier).

## Two deliberate design choices

**Nothing in this set can be satisfied by the corpus writing more corpus.** Every measurement is either a count over existing files and git history or an experiment run *outside* the corpus (re-check in a fresh context, task test with a fresh agent, the authority's own self-report). That is the direct response to Campbell's law, which applies with unusual force to a system that defines itself: run these once, as a diagnosis, by someone who does not own the corpus. Adopting them as standing screens inside `basis/` would make them the fourteenth check and would confirm the pathology they exist to detect.

**Two hypotheses look already answered by the observables, and one looks mis-stated.** H3 is confirmed on count (zero quality-attribute vocabulary across 115 files). H4 has direct evidence (196 `self-check` occurrences, maker-stamped `checked` features, self-asserted pass tables, an "Accepted tradeoffs" section declining repair of the founding set's own violations). H1 is the one to be careful with: the honest version is not verbosity but obligation count and unreproducible judgment — DORA's documentation-quality findings are among the strongest effect sizes in delivery research, and RegData's contribution was showing restriction counts track burden where page counts do not. A finding of "too many words" that cannot be restated as obligations-per-step, unserved rules, or a findability failure is not supported by any source in this brief.

factors.name: Delivered output versus artifacts about output
factors.question: How much definition mass exists per unit of thing the definitions exist to produce, is the ratio moving toward delivery, and is there a declared appetite that could ever trip a circuit breaker?
factors.measurement: Partition every word, commit and hour into (A) product-facing output consumed outside the system that produced it, (B) definitions/process/tooling about how work is done, (C) records about work done. Report (B+C)/total weekly so the derivative is visible, plus elapsed days ÷ declared appetite. Re-run baselines (verified 2026-09-17): `find basis -name '*.md' | wc -l` → 115 files; `cat $(find basis -name '*.md') | wc -w` → 159,891 words; plus ~130k more words in requests/, briefs/, decisions/, features/, initiatives/, sessions/; `find . -name '*.py' | xargs wc -l` → 4,461 lines, all of it corpus compilers, linters and cost rollups (basis/tools/); 280 commits since 2026-08-22; product-facing software: zero. A = 0, so the ratio is 1.0. Then: count efforts with a written appetite, efforts past appetite, and of those how many were cancelled rather than extended — Shape Up's circuit breaker leaves a record of things killed; no such record in 26 days means the model is cited, not in force.
factors.sources: Agile Manifesto, Principles 1/3/7 — "Working software is the primary measure of progress" (https://agilemanifesto.org/principles.html); Ryan Singer, Shape Up ch. 6 (appetite) and ch. 8 ("If they don't finish, by default the project doesn't get an extension") — https://basecamp.com/shapeup/2.2-chapter-08; Hamel & Zanini, "What We Learned About Bureaucracy from 7,000 HBR Readers", HBR Aug 2017 (insularity = effort on internal rather than external issues) — https://hbr.org/2017/08/what-we-learned-about-bureaucracy-from-7000-hbr-readers; Dan Ward, The Simplicity Cycle (2015) — complexity raises goodness to an inflection point and lowers it after.

factors.name: Coverage of the built artifact versus coverage of the procedure
factors.question: Does the corpus say anywhere what a good built thing looks like, or only who does what, in what order, checked by whom?
factors.measurement: Classify every directive as artifact-quality (a property of the thing produced: decomposition, interfaces, failure behaviour, performance, security, readability) or process-quality (sequence, record, role, check). Report the ratio per principle set and corpus-wide. Then map the corpus onto ISO/IEC 25010:2023's nine characteristics and count how many are addressed with stated criteria. Coverage test: take five questions a maker actually asks — how do I decompose this, what belongs behind an interface, how should errors surface, when is duplication acceptable, what does done mean for this scenario — and count how many the corpus answers. Verified baseline: `grep -ril <term> basis --include='*.md'` gives maintainability 0, modular 0, cohesion 0, reliability 0, security 0, coupling 1, performance 3, testab* 5, observab* 5 files. All six implementation principles (built-to-the-scenario, effect-shown, effect-not-mechanism, nothing-lost, knowable-from-the-record, cost-on-the-initiative) govern scope, evidence and accounting; none states a property of well-built software.
factors.sources: ISO/IEC 25010:2023, Systems and software engineering — SQuaRE — Product quality model, nine characteristics (https://www.iso.org/standard/78176.html; 2023 change summary https://quality.arc42.org/articles/iso-25010-update-2023); TOGAF Architecture Principles, "Complete" and "Robust" criteria (https://pubs.opengroup.org/architecture/togaf92-doc/arch/chap20.html); Jeff Bezos, 2017 Letter to Shareholders — "high standards are teachable" only if people can "recognize what excellence looks like in a domain" (https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/2017-letter-to-shareholders).

factors.name: Enforcement locus: tooled gate versus prose rule
factors.question: For each obligation, what actually stops a violation — a schema, a tool, a failing test — or only a sentence the agent is asked to remember?
factors.measurement: Tabulate every normative statement against its enforcement level: (1) structurally impossible to violate, (2) blocked by tool/schema/lint at write time, (3) detected automatically after the fact, (4) checked by a fresh-context agent against stated criteria, (5) prose only, self-attested. Report the distribution, and for every level 4–5 rule ask whether a violation produces any signal at all. Verified baseline: 127 MUST/MUST NOT statements in basis/ (`grep -rho '\bMUST\b' basis --include='*.md' | wc -l` → 106; MUST NOT → 21) against basis/tools/lint_basis.py, whose entire rule surface is ~53 definitions/error sites — i.e. most obligations sit at level 4–5. Second count: obligations that are about form, presence, naming, sequence or completeness (a linter's natural class) but are enforced by prose — each one is context spent on something a program could enforce at zero context cost.
factors.sources: Anthropic, "Building effective agents" (Dec 2024) — "Poka-yoke your tools. Change the arguments so that it is harder to make mistakes" (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents); Anthropic, "Effective harnesses for long-running agents" — structure the environment rather than the prompt; forbid status changes until an external test runs; OpenAI, "A practical guide to building agents" (Apr 2025), layered guardrails mixing deterministic and model-based checks (https://cdn.openai.com/business-guides-and-resources/a-practical-guide-to-building-agents.pdf); Zhou et al., IFEval, arXiv:2311.07911 — the tractable instruction class is the programmatically verifiable one.

factors.name: Constraint integrity: who can waive, who can stamp
factors.question: Can the party a constraint binds relieve itself of that constraint, or declare its own work compliant, without any other party acting?
factors.measurement: Build the unrule register. Table: constraint | binds whom | who may waive | waivers in the last 30 days | where the waiver is recorded | expiry | ever revisited. Grep the corpus and working artifacts for `accepted gap`, `accepted tradeoff`, `exception`, `waiver`, `deferred`, `out of scope for now`, `not repaired`, and for self-asserted fitness-pass tables. Report (a) unrules per obligation, (b) share invoked by the same role the obligation constrains, (c) share with no expiry and no owner, (d) age of each. Separately classify every check's checker as: same agent, different role but same generating context and same interest in passing, fresh context with different accountability, or external. Then the asymmetry test: process weight to impose an obligation (draft, guideline, fitness set, independent judge, owner approval) versus process weight to lift one. Verified baseline: `grep -ro 'self-check' --include='*.md' . | wc -l` → 196 occurrences; `accepted gap` appears across 8 files including basis/artifacts/feature.md and six feature records; basis/principles.md follows its self-asserted fitness screen with an "Accepted tradeoffs" section recording known violations of the set's own rules and declining repair; features are set `checked` by the PO that authored them; the artifact tooling exists but nothing prevents a raw sed/grep edit around it (greppable in session transcripts).
factors.sources: Coglianese, Scheffler & Walters, "Unrules", 73 Stan. L. Rev. 885 (2021) — "A regulatory system can be understood only as the net effects of both its rules and its unrules"; constraints on imposing obligations exceed constraints on lifting them (https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2021/04/Coglianese-et-al.-73-Stan.-L.-Rev.-885.pdf); IIA, The Three Lines Model (July 2020) — assurance requires independence from the activity assessed (https://www.theiia.org/globalassets/documents/resources/the-iias-three-lines-model-an-update-of-the-three-lines-of-defense-july-2020/three-lines-model-updated-english.pdf); ISO 9001 cl. 9.2 / ISO 19011 impartiality; Cai et al., "Rule Taxonomy and Evolution in AI IDEs", arXiv:2606.12231 — baseline artifact compliance with stated rules 49.14% across 83 projects and 7,310 rules.

factors.name: Feedback from outcome back to specification
factors.question: For any definition in this corpus, is there a recorded before/after outcome showing it changed behaviour for the better — and does any error signal reach the corpus from outside the corpus?
factors.measurement: Count definitions with any outcome measure attached (an A/B, a before/after defect or compliance count, a rework count), as a percentage of all definitions. Record time since each definition's last outcome measurement and the number of revisions made with no outcome evidence. Count the eval fixtures that exist at all — representative tasks the corpus can be run against. Then classify every indicator the system uses (approvals granted, checks passed, fitness screens cleared, self-checks recorded) as self-reported by the measured party or independently observed, and plot each against any externally observable outcome. Verified baseline: 18 features, 16 initiatives, 10 ADRs, 8 PDRs, 41 requests, 29 session records — every recorded indicator is internal and self-reported; the only external observable (shipped software) is flat at zero, so no indicator can be correlated with anything outside the loop.
factors.sources: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov & Suhr, "Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design", ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.11324 — semantically equivalent formatting variants swing accuracy up to 76 points, so untested wording is an untested intervention; Gloaguen et al., "Evaluating AGENTS.md", arXiv:2602.11988 — context files gave no general success gain at >20% inference cost; "any attempts to improve performance should be rigorously evaluated before deployment"; Agrawal et al., GEPA, arXiv:2507.19457 and Zhou et al., APE, arXiv:2211.01910 — author intuition about instruction wording is a poor predictor; V. F. Ridgway, "Dysfunctional Consequences of Performance Measurements", ASQ 1(2) 1956; Meyer & Rowan, AJS 83(2) 1977 — decoupling sustained by a "logic of confidence".

factors.name: Form fit: rule, standard or principle — and does the form match the traffic?
factors.question: For each normative statement, was its content fixed in advance (a rule) or left to be given content at the point of application (a standard/principle) — does that choice match how often and how uniformly the situation arises, and can the corpus express any form but the rule?
factors.measurement: Tabulate every normative statement. (a) Classify rule vs standard: can a reader decide compliance from the text alone, or must someone judge at the moment of use? (b) Count actual applications in the last 30 days from the working artifacts — how many times did this statement bind real work? Score two mismatch buckets: rules applied 0–2 times (content fixed in advance for traffic that never came; report their total word cost) and standards applied 20+ times (the same judgment re-litigated every session). (c) Classify every directive into Sunstein's forms — untrammeled discretion, rules, rules with excuses, presumptions, factors, standards, guidelines, principles — and report the histogram; count how many forms the corpus can express at all. A corpus with no presumption, no factor list, and no documented-departure guideline has a one-form grammar. (d) Report the share of directives labelled "principle" that are in fact rules by Sunstein's test; in this corpus the principle-set typedef's own construction (a principle as a standing rule, statements binary-testable on one artifact) makes that share close to 100% by design. (e) Search Document History and briefs for guidance-style content dropped because it would not fit the rule form.
factors.sources: Louis Kaplow, "Rules versus Standards: An Economic Analysis", 42 Duke L.J. 557 (1992), pp. 560, 577, 599–600 — "the only distinction between rules and standards is the extent to which efforts to give content to the law are undertaken before or after individuals act"; "the greater the frequency with which a legal command will apply, the more desirable rules tend to be relative to standards" (https://scholarship.law.duke.edu/dlj/vol42/iss3/2/); Cass R. Sunstein, "Problems with Rules", 83 Calif. L. Rev. 953 (1995), pp. 959–68 — "a principle is a background notion that does not by itself cover an individual case... principles tend to bear on cases without disposing of them" (p. 966); "If a standard is transparent... it is a rule" (p. 965) (https://scholarship.law.berkeley.edu/californialawreview/vol83/iss4/1/); TOGAF Architecture Principles, "Consistent" — the set "must be expressed in a way that allows a balance of interpretations".

factors.name: Obligation load per activity, for the human and the model reader
factors.question: How many independently checkable obligations bind one step at once, how much text must be traversed to find them, and does adherence hold at that count?
factors.measurement: Count obligations, not sentences: every clause a checker could independently mark pass/fail that binds this step — compiled principle bullets, guideline writing rules, typedef fields, fitness criteria, step prompt directives. Sum per step and record which are always-on (inherited) versus local; flag any step whose always-on share exceeds ~30% of its load. Report words per obligation, mean sentence length and sentences over 30 words, and the structural-overhead ratio: words about the corpus's own mechanics (types, chains, renderings, compilations, load points) over words about the product or the work. Then run the empirical half: take 10 recent outputs produced under that context, score each against every obligation, and compare against the same agent given only the 5 most load-bearing obligations — if the extra rules buy no measurable quality, they are cost with no yield. Verified baselines: 25 process definitions totalling 63,009 words; normative keywords in basis/ 106 MUST, 21 MUST NOT, 5 SHOULD, 0 SHOULD NOT, 13 MAY (absolute share 88%, MUST:SHOULD ≈ 21:1); repo-wide 157/28/5/13 (absolute share 91%). Note the researchers' counts differ from mine (129/28 vs 106/21) depending on scope — re-run the grep and state the scope rather than inheriting a number. Apply RFC 2119 §6 to a sample of MUSTs: does this exist for interoperation between roles or to prevent harm, or is it method imposition?
factors.sources: UK Office of the Parliamentary Counsel, Drafting Guidance (March 2024) 1.1.11 ("one idea per sentence"), 1.1.13–14 ("The medium is not the message"), 1.3.2 (Gowers) — https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/660407d091a320001a82b06b/2024.03.19.Drafting-guidance.pdf; Jaroslawicz et al., IFScale, arXiv:2507.11538 — adherence degrades steadily with instruction count, omission errors dominating, with primacy bias toward earlier instructions; Kimura et al., ManyIFEval, EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv:2509.21051 — all-instructions-satisfied accuracy predictable from count alone; Anthropic, "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (Sept 2025) — "the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens" (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents); RFC 2119 §6 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.txt); Al-Ubaydli & McLaughlin, RegData, Regulation & Governance 11(1) 2017 — restriction counts track burden better than page counts.

factors.name: Rejection power and contestability
factors.question: Shown the last 20–30 pieces of real work, how much would each principle have turned away — how much did it actually turn away on the record — and could a competent peer shop defend its opposite?
factors.measurement: Two numbers per principle: hypothetical rejection rate (of the last 20–30 delivered artifacts, how many would it have rejected) and observed rejection rate (a check that failed and cited this principle, a review finding, a rewrite). Spool's benchmark is roughly two-thirds hypothetical; an observed rate of zero over the whole corpus history means the principle has never changed an output. Then contestability: write each principle's negation as a one-line position and score contested (a named real practice holds it and survives) / permission-to-play (no competent shop would hold the negation) / vacuous (the negation is unintelligible). Cheap proxies: count principles whose statement contains no trade-off ("rather than", "over", "instead of", a named cost accepted); count obligations per principle statement (five MUST bullets is five stands, not one); count principles whose rationale contains no concrete failure example. Structural hazard to flag here: basis/guidelines/principle-set.md forbids grounding a rationale in the product's own operational history — which is precisely the evidence Spool's Test #1 demands, so no principle in this corpus can prove it came from research.
factors.sources: Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design Principles: 6 Counter-Intuitive Tests" — Test #1 comes from research, Test #2 "Does it Help You Say 'No' Most of the Time?", Test #4 reversibility (https://articles.centercentre.com/creating-design-principles/); Patrick Lencioni, "Make Your Values Mean Something", HBR July 2002 — permission-to-play values "never really help distinguish a company" and bland sets are "highly destructive" (https://hbr.org/2002/07/make-your-values-mean-something); Charlie Kindel, "Tenets" (2020) — a tenet "takes a stand by declaring that a team cares more about one thing than another" (https://blog.kindel.com/2020/02/10/tenets/); Richard Rumelt, Good Strategy / Bad Strategy (2011) — fluff, "Sunday words", the guiding policy that "directs and constrains action without fully defining it".

factors.name: Check economics: does each check pay, and is its verdict reproducible?
factors.question: What fraction of effort goes into checking rather than making, how often does each check actually fail anything, and would a fresh context re-checking the same artifact reach the same verdict?
factors.measurement: Per standing check: items checked in the last 30 days, items failed, hours spent, estimated cost of an escape. Defect fraction p = failed ÷ checked; compare against Deming's kp break-even (inspect none if p < k1/k2). A check with a 100% historical pass rate is either redundant with the making step or performed pro forma. Count check steps per process definition and the number of distinct checks one artifact passes end to end; count checks that cannot cite the clause they enforce. Then reproducibility: take 5 artifacts recorded as passing, re-run the stated check in a fresh context with no access to the original verdict, and report the agreement rate (healthy ≥80%, red <60%) and whether the check can be re-run at all or exists only as a prose assertion. Same test as an inter-reader agreement measure: 10 rules × 10 artifacts, two fresh contexts, yes/no verdict plus the clause relied on — rules under ~80% agreement are standards wearing a rule's clothes, paying a rule's promulgation cost and a standard's interpretation cost. Verified baseline: every process definition in basis/processes/ ends in or contains check steps (`grep -c check` ranges 2–63 per file across 25 files); basis/architecture-principles.md and basis/implementation-principles.md each end in an in-document fitness screen whose rows read "pass", asserted by the author — an unreproducible pass by construction.
factors.sources: W. Edwards Deming, Out of the Crisis (1986), Point 3 — "Cease dependence on inspection... build quality into the product in the first place" (https://deming.org/explore/fourteen-points/) and the kp all-or-none inspection criterion, J. Quality Technology 17(3) 1985; Michael Power, The Audit Society: Rituals of Verification (OUP 1997) — audit produces comfort rather than knowledge and "self-referentially creat[es] auditable images of performance"; Cemri, Pan, Yang et al., MAST, arXiv:2503.13657 — task-verification failure (premature termination, inadequate verification) is one of three top failure categories over 1,600+ annotated traces; Julia Black, "Forms and Paradoxes of Principles Based Regulation", LSE WP 13/2008, pp. 22–24, 29–31 — the interpretive and enforcement paradoxes; Colin S. Diver, "The Optimal Precision of Administrative Rules", 93 Yale L.J. 65 (1983).

factors.name: Flow efficiency, the single-human constraint, and batch size
factors.question: Of the elapsed time from a request entering to something leaving, what fraction added value — how much of that elapsed time was queued in front of the one human, and how big is the unit of work between contacts with reality?
factors.measurement: Take 5 completed items end to end from commit and session timestamps; mark each interval touch or wait (waiting on approval, clarification, a check, a rendering). Flow efficiency = touch ÷ elapsed (practitioner reference band: 5–15% typical, 15–25% good; treat as a within-system trend, not a gate). Governance variant: fraction of touch time spent on the item versus on satisfying the process about the item — red if the second exceeds the first. Constraint: count process steps requiring the authority's decision as a share of all steps; items waiting on that person; mean wait per approval; and the split of the authority's attention between irreducible decisions (bets, direction, priority) and reducible clarifications (what does this rule mean, does this satisfy that). The discriminator is the trend in clarification share across successive artifacts — falling means the corpus is maturing, flat or rising means each new definition buys ambiguity at least as fast as it resolves it. Batch size: how many artifacts are approved in one decision (this corpus approved the product flow end to end "by batch under brief-032"), and the interval between a corpus change and any external validation — currently unbounded, since nothing has executed. Alongside these, record the authority's own standing self-report (is this getting easier or harder; what fraction of last cycle moved the product): in a one-human system that perception is the outcome variable, not anecdote.
factors.sources: Eliyahu Goldratt, The Goal (1984) and the Five Focusing Steps, esp. "subordinate" — non-constraints must not run faster than the constraint (https://www.tocinstitute.org/five-focusing-steps.html); Kanban University, "Flow Efficiency" (https://resources.kanban.university/flow-efficiency-a-great-metric-you-probably-arent-using/); Donald Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) — batch size economics and invisible queues; Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Houck & Butler, "The SPACE of Developer Productivity", ACM Queue 19(1) 2021 — use at least three dimensions, never one metric, include perceptual data (https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3454124).

factors.name: Ceremonial mass: definitions never executed, rules never retired
factors.question: How many defined processes have actually run end to end, how long after approval did the first run happen, and how many obligations have ever been removed?
factors.measurement: Per definition: date approved → date first executed end to end; number of complete executions; date of last execution; steps skipped in the most recent execution; and whether any record asserts a step ran that left no artifact. Compute never-run share (red flag >40%) and median definition-to-execution lag. From version control, count obligations added, amended and removed per week and compute the retirement ratio = removals ÷ additions; also rule half-life (median age at first revisit). A monotonic rule count is the expected null trajectory for any rule-making system, so the retirement ratio is the only observable separating learning from silting. Verified baseline: 25 process definitions, 63,009 words; several (implementation, scenario-assignment, reconcile-and-close, the bc-emit and mailbox paths) are unexecutable by construction while the shop is frozen, yet stand fully specified and approved; git history over 280 commits shows additive approval batches and no recorded retirement event in the corpus's own terms — retirement exists only as a planned migration action. Also apply Bozeman's test to 10 randomly sampled obligations: name one concrete failure this rule prevented in the last 30 days, with the record that shows it; red-tape share = (unserved + unknown) ÷ 10.
factors.sources: James G. March, Martin Schulz & Xueguang Zhou, The Dynamics of Rules: Change in Written Organizational Codes (Stanford UP, 2000) — rule birth is easy, rule suspension rare (https://www.sup.org/books/title/?id=388); Barry Bozeman, Bureaucracy and Red Tape (2000) — red tape as rules that "remain in force and entail a compliance burden but [do] not advance the legitimate purposes the rules were intended to serve"; rule-inception versus rule-evolved red tape (overview: https://regulatorystudies.columbian.gwu.edu/red-tape-literature-public-administration); John W. Meyer & Brian Rowan, "Institutionalized Organizations: Formal Structure as Myth and Ceremony", AJS 83(2) 1977 — ceremonial adoption and decoupling of formal structure from activity.

factors.name: Fidelity of adopted external forms
factors.question: Where the corpus cites an external standard, does it adopt that standard as the source defines it, and is every narrowing, inversion or home-grown addition recorded as a reasoned departure?
factors.measurement: For each external source the corpus names, put the source's own criteria in one column and the corpus's rendering in the next; mark each adopted / narrowed / inverted / dropped, and require a recorded justification for each narrowing. Score fidelity as the share adopted intact. Flag hardest any criterion in a fitness screen that traces to no named source — under the corpus's own external-standards-first principle, a bespoke criterion must be justified by a recorded gap in the form it rejects. Verified starting points in this corpus: basis/fitness/principle-set.fitness.md states its tests "compose TOGAF (statement quality), Spool (helps you say no), Lencioni (not permission-to-play)", and basis/guidelines/principle-set.md cites TOGAF and operational definitions — so check whether TOGAF's Consistent ("allows a balance of interpretations"), Robust and Stable survived; whether Spool's Test #1 (comes from research) survived a guideline that bans product operational history from rationales, and whether Test #4 (reversibility) appears at all; whether BCP 14 was adopted with its §6 necessity limit; and whether any criterion of the form "implies at least one practice and at least one check" has an external parent — that clause is the one that converts a principle set into a generator of process mass.
factors.sources: TOGAF Architecture Principles — the five set-level criteria and the 10–20 heuristic (https://pubs.opengroup.org/architecture/togaf92-doc/arch/chap20.html); Spool's six tests in full (https://articles.centercentre.com/creating-design-principles/); Lencioni's four value types (https://hbr.org/2002/07/make-your-values-mean-something); RFC 2119 §6 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.txt) and RFC 8174 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174.txt); W3C RfcKeywords — keywords attach to a conformance object performing a specified operation (https://www.w3.org/wiki/RfcKeywords); Rumelt's kernel requiring a diagnosis before any guiding policy.

factors.name: Decode cost and findability
factors.question: Can the agent or human who needs a definition find it, parse it, and trust it to be current — or must they reconcile four documents at three levels of a chain to assemble one obligation?
factors.measurement: Task test, not opinion: give a fresh agent 5 real tasks; record time-to-locate the governing definition, number of documents opened, and whether the answer found was current. Multiple documents needing reconciliation to answer one question is a findability failure even when every document is individually correct. Decode cost: take five representative sentences from process definitions and count how many defined terms a reader must already know to parse each — four or more lookups marks the sentence for plain-word rewriting. Per glossary term and schema element: uses outside its own definition (fewer than three marks it for deletion), uses where an ordinary word would carry the same meaning, and any definition that smuggles an obligation into itself rather than stating it as an operative provision. Staleness: share of documents whose stated source-digest or referenced definition no longer matches (this corpus stamps digests, so the check is mechanical). Also classify each paragraph as (a) non-obvious local constraint, (b) restatement of something defined elsewhere in the corpus, (c) restatement of general good practice the model already knows, (d) rationale addressed to humans, and report the (a)-share — the field evidence says (a) is the part that pays and (b)/(c) is the part that costs without paying.
factors.sources: DORA, Capabilities: Documentation quality — clarity, findability, reliability; quality documentation amplifies the organisational-performance effect of every technical capability studied (https://dora.dev/capabilities/documentation-quality/); UK OPC, Drafting Guidance (March 2024) Part 4.1 — avoid misleading labels (4.1.4), avoid bland labels (4.1.5), "Don't make a definition do too much" (4.1.8–9) (https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/660407d091a320001a82b06b/2024.03.19.Drafting-guidance.pdf); Gloaguen et al., "Evaluating AGENTS.md", arXiv:2602.11988 — instructions are followed but repository overviews are not helpful; removing duplicated docs turned a negative into +2.7%; Bryan A. Garner, Legal Writing in Plain English (3rd ed., 2023).

data.rationale:
## Shape of the set

Thirteen factors, ordered so the five foundational ones answer the restart question on their own and the rest explain why. The organising claim is that this corpus has three independent failure surfaces — **what it says** (form and coverage), **what makes it stick** (enforcement and waiver), and **what tells it it is wrong** (outcome feedback and delivery) — and that the third is the one that makes the other two unrecoverable. So `delivery-vs-definition-mass`, `artifact-quality-coverage`, `enforcement-locus`, `constraint-integrity` and `outcome-feedback-loop` are foundational: if all five fail, no per-rule improvement can help, because nothing outside the corpus can tell the corpus it is wrong, nothing in it constrains the product, and nothing but prose holds any rule in place.

Every factor is countable against this repository, and I re-ran the baselines rather than inheriting them. Confirmed on `rebaseline` at 2026-09-17: 115 markdown files / 159,891 words in `basis/`; 25 process definitions totalling 63,009 words; 4,461 lines of Python, all of it corpus compilers, linters and cost rollups; 280 commits since 2026-08-22; zero product-facing software. Normative keywords in `basis/`: **106 MUST, 21 MUST NOT, 5 SHOULD, 0 SHOULD NOT, 13 MAY** (repo-wide 157/28/5/13). The researchers quoted 129/28 — the gap is scope, and I left the exact grep in the measurement so the number is re-derived, not quoted. Quality-attribute vocabulary in `basis/`: maintainability 0 files, modular 0, cohesion 0, reliability 0, security 0, coupling 1, performance 3. `self-check` appears 196 times; `accepted gap` across 8 files. `lint_basis.py` carries roughly 53 rule sites against 127 MUST/MUST NOT statements.

## What I merged

- **Four separate ratio factors** (time to first output, promulgation-to-delivery, meta-work, corpus-to-output) collapse into one, with Shape Up's circuit breaker folded in as a measurement: an appetite nobody can trip is the same finding as a ratio nobody watches.
- **Independence of the check** merged into `constraint-integrity` rather than standing with check economics. Self-approval and self-waiver are one phenomenon: the maker relieving itself. Splitting them lets a system pass one and fail the other while the defect is identical.
- **Reproducibility of a verdict** and **independent-application agreement** are the same experiment (fresh context, same artifact, compare) applied to checks and to rules; they sit together in `check-economics` as its empirical half. That experiment is the single highest-yield thing a reviewer can run here — five re-runs settle an argument that would otherwise run for weeks.
- **Rule-form fit (Kaplow)** and **position on the discretion continuum (Sunstein)** merged into `form-fit`. Kaplow prices the form against traffic; Sunstein names the forms. Separately they invite the trap the cautions warn about — Kaplow alone can be read as "write more rules".
- **Obligation count for models** and **idea density for humans** merged into one factor. They are the same count with two bodies of evidence behind them, and keeping them apart would have implied the corpus could be tuned for one reader at the other's expense.
- **Rule retirement**, **definition-to-execution lag**, **never-run processes** and **red tape** merged into `ceremonial-mass`: all four measure definition written for activity that has not happened and is not disciplined by contact with execution. In a frozen shop with fully specified dispatch, assignment and reconcile processes, this is one finding, not four.

## What I dropped, and why

- **Conflict surface / stated precedence.** Genuine design smell, but the only field study (McMillan, 1,650 sessions) returned an affirmative null for adjacent-file contradiction (BF10 0.05–0.10). A factor whose effect size is contested does not belong in a set that has to carry a restart decision.
- **Prohibition framing.** Self-nominated by its own author as the weakest-sourced factor, resting on practitioner analysis rather than a study. The MUST:SHOULD:MAY count in `obligation-load` already catches the register problem.
- **Within-session compliance decay** as a standalone factor. It is the best-supported field finding in the whole brief (OR 0.944 per generated function) but it rates *how work is scheduled*, not the corpus. It survives as the reason `check-economics` insists on fresh contexts.
- **Instruction altitude** and **output-contract concreteness.** Both are prompt-engineering quality, and both are largely downstream of `form-fit` and `artifact-quality-coverage`: a corpus with no exemplars of a good built thing has no output contract to give.
- **Governance debt ratio (SQALE).** Attractive for the restart arithmetic, but remediation effort is an estimate, and the brief's own rule is that factors deciding a restart must carry hard counts. `delivery-vs-definition-mass` plus `ceremonial-mass` give the same answer from observables.
- **Handoff payload completeness** and **loaded-context budget** as standalone factors, folded into `obligation-load` (always-on share) and `check-economics` (fresh-context carrier).

## Two deliberate design choices

**Nothing in this set can be satisfied by the corpus writing more corpus.** Every measurement is either a count over existing files and git history or an experiment run *outside* the corpus (re-check in a fresh context, task test with a fresh agent, the authority's own self-report). That is the direct response to Campbell's law, which applies with unusual force to a system that defines itself: run these once, as a diagnosis, by someone who does not own the corpus. Adopting them as standing screens inside `basis/` would make them the fourteenth check and would confirm the pathology they exist to detect.

**Two hypotheses look already answered by the observables, and one looks mis-stated.** H3 is confirmed on count (zero quality-attribute vocabulary across 115 files). H4 has direct evidence (196 `self-check` occurrences, maker-stamped `checked` features, self-asserted pass tables, an "Accepted tradeoffs" section declining repair of the founding set's own violations). H1 is the one to be careful with: the honest version is not verbosity but obligation count and unreproducible judgment — DORA's documentation-quality findings are among the strongest effect sizes in delivery research, and RegData's contribution was showing restriction counts track burden where page counts do not. A finding of "too many words" that cannot be restated as obligations-per-step, unserved rules, or a findability failure is not supported by any source in this brief.
